####  The purpose of this script is to explore complex plotting ideas by making some absolutely horrid figures, then making a more acceptable one.

##  Libraries
```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(lubridate)
library(tidytuesdayR)
library(maps)
library(mapdata)
library(mapproj)
library(plotly)
```

##  Data
```{r}
#| message: false
tuesdata <- tidytuesdayR::tt_load(2026, week = 36)
# ^ tidytuesday data requires you to load in both the dfs of the week
# v and read in the dataset you're interested in
cafe <- tuesdata$cafe
# This dataset comes with a 2nd df indexing labor-hours
cappuccino_index <- tuesdata$cappuccino_index

#NZ and South Africa have spaces in their contry codes that mess up mapping data, so the TT post has this to clean it:
cappuccino_index$country <- gsub("\u00a0", " ", cappuccino_index$country)
```

*Taking a look at the data*
```{r}
#| message: false
#| eval: false
str(cafe)
str(cappuccino_index)

glimpse(cafe)
glimpse(cappuccino_index)
```
*Functions*
```{r}
#adding phycount() because it can be used for Countries and stuff too!
phycount = function(data, taxa) { 
  df <- data |>
    select({{taxa}}) |>
    drop_na() |>
    group_by({{taxa}}) |>
    summarize(member_count = n()) |>
    arrange(desc(member_count))
    return(df)
}
```

__Bad plot functions__
*This sets up the mask for where dots can live on the plot*
```{r}
#Found this silhoutteing plotting method from the TidyTuesday's frog data winner!

#Uploaded	2022 Aug 23 by T. Michael Keesey
#Coffea arabica
silhouette <- png::readPNG(curl::curl_fetch_memory("https://images.phylopic.org/images/d792cf69-7fa9-4340-a8a4-20102b09ab25/raster/1086x1536.png?v=182ecbbb7bd")$content)
coffee_mask <- silhouette[, , dim(silhouette)[3]] > 0.5

city_ct <- phycount(cafe, city)
#condenses counts down to not make tiny dots
things_per_dot <- 1
n_thing <- nrow(city_ct)
n_dots <- ceiling(n_thing / things_per_dot)

# Hexagonal grid of candidate dot positions, in pixel coordinates
hex_grid <- function(spacing) {
  expand_grid(i = 0:(nrow(coffee_mask) %/% (spacing * sqrt(3) / 2)), j = 0:(ncol(coffee_mask) %/% spacing)) |>
    mutate(row = 1 + i * spacing * sqrt(3) / 2, x = 1 + j * spacing + ((i + 1) %% 2) * spacing / 2) |>
    filter(row <= nrow(coffee_mask), x <= ncol(coffee_mask)) |>
    filter(coffee_mask[cbind(round(row), round(x))]) |>
    mutate(y = nrow(coffee_mask) - row)
} #my brain is melted from the math parts of this

#Making gaps in the spacing that allows all dots to be split nicely
dot_spacing <- detect(seq(60, 10, by = -0.05), \(s) nrow(hex_grid(s)) >= n_dots)

#Converts the detected spacing into a dataframe with all the plotting data for putting hexagonal dots through a mask layer
dots <- hex_grid(dot_spacing) |>
  mutate(neighbours = rowSums(as.matrix(dist(pick(x, y))) < dot_spacing * 1.1)) |>
  slice_max(neighbours, n = n_dots, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  arrange(x, y)

#We have to add our city names back into the df, otherwise we're gonna have loose points with nothing in them!
cafe_dots <- dots |>
  mutate(city = city_ct$city[seq(1, n_thing, by = things_per_dot)])
  

```
*Plotting*
```{r}
for_plotly <- ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = cafe_dots, aes(x, y, color = city), size = dot_spacing * 0.08, stroke = 0) +
  #using our point data to lock the x and y coordinates, our only real variable is city.
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.1, 0.01))) +
  coord_fixed(clip = "off") +
  #stuff to make the image behave
  guides(color = "none") +
  theme_void() +
    theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "black", color = NA))
  #makes the plot dark and empty, like a Hot Topic employee
  
#Absuing ggplotly once more to make something illegible have some plausible readability
plot <- ggplotly(for_plotly) |>
  layout(plot_bgcolor = "black",
         paper_bgcolor = "black")
  #ggplotly tries to escape the darkness inside, but luckily I've got a new bottle of mascara and black nail polish

plot #naming it something super generic in code, because why think so hard! There's no way this can backfire!
```
Now **this** is vile!  \
\
The colors represent the distribution of cities in this study about coffee shops. Lovingly plotted against the silhouette of a coffee branch!
\
Some massive rules broken:

- Data is organized by biggest city on the left (which is extra hard to tell with the leaf structures and a crazy grid)
- The color scaling is so janky when you go between the cities with similar counts and ones that have 1 entry
- Black background + awful colors make this look like a Lite-Brite, to appeal to 80s kids
- No axis, no title, no info on what this even is
- You can see which cities are in the study simply by mousing over! Why not find your favorite one while this is on a monitor at a conference? I'm sure it'll be easy, and not at all infuriating
- You get a useless x and y axis value when you mouse over, just so you know where on this plot your city is! (Share with your colleges!)

__Good Plot__
*Wrangling data, loading maps*
```{r}
world <- map_data("world") #loading in world map data

#Making a usful plot of the cappuccino_index by country, so we can see the disparity between labor value and coffee value, first we have to combine the map data with the cappuccino index.
cap_in <- cappuccino_index #I already misspelled cappuccino 5 times making this, no longer!

world_cap <- cap_in |>
  select("region" = country, index, index_as_time) |> #changinges "country" to match the mapping df's "region"
  inner_join(world)
```
*Plotting*
```{r}
cap_print <- ggplot() +
    geom_polygon(data = world,
               aes(x = long, y = lat,
                   group = group,
                   ), fill = "white") +
    guides(fill = "none") +
    geom_polygon(data = world_cap,
               aes(x = long, y = lat,
                   group = group,
                   fill = log(index), #Have to transform the data to really see differences, otherwise the India/Pakistan region outweighs the data.
                   text = paste0(region, 
                                      "<br>", index_as_time)),
               color = "black", linewidth = 0.1) +
  theme_void() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "lightgreen", high = "maroon") +
  coord_map(projection = "mercator",
            xlim = c(-180, 180)) +
  #coord_fixed(1.25) +
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "lightblue")) +
  labs(title = "Cappuchino Index",
       subtitle = "Heatmap of Barista labor:product disparity",
       caption = "From James Hoffman, data curated by Filip Reierson",
       #fill = "Capp price / Barista Wage"
       )
#annoyingly, plotly doesn't read Labs so I have to make my own
cap_print
#going to post the original plot as well

#ggsave(here("Week_08", "output", "Cupp_index_map.png"))
```
Much nicer!  \
\
This Good Plot logartythmically transforms the data so it's easier to see the smaller differences, as well as color coordinating what's ultimately an inference of work-life standards, but also inequality across the globe.  \
\
It's interesting to see that the countries that produce the most coffee beans have a worse labor:cup rating than ones that roast beans and produce value-added products.




*Making on online widget to visualize the data better*
```{r}

#in order to try fixing the plotly image, it's better to re-make the ggplot

cap_ly <- ggplot() +
    geom_polygon(data = world,
               aes(x = long, y = lat,
                   group = group,
                   ), fill = "gray") +
    guides(fill = "none") +
    geom_polygon(data = world_cap,
               aes(x = long, y = lat,
                   group = group,
                   fill = log(index), #Have to transform the data to really see differences, otherwise the India/Pakistan region outweighs the data.
                   text = paste0(region, 
                                      "<br>", index_as_time)),
               color = "black", linewidth = 0.1) +
  theme_void() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "lightgreen", high = "maroon") +
  #coord_map(projection = "mercator",
           # xlim = c(-180, 180)) +
  coord_fixed(1.25) + #This is better for making the widget than coor_map, yet not perfect
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "lightblue")) +
  labs(title = "Cappuchino Index",
       subtitle = "Labor hours it takes for a barista to pay for one cappuchino in their own country",
       caption = "From James Hoffman, data curated by Filip Reierson")
#annoyingly, plotly doesn't read Labs so I have to make my own

cap_interactive <- ggplotly(cap_ly, tooltip = "text") |>
  layout(
    title = list(
      text = paste0(
        "Cappuchino Index", 
        "<br>", 
        "<sup>Labor hours it takes for a barista to pay for one cappuchino in their own country</sup>")),
    margin = list(b=80) #stackoverflow said this could help, but I can't tell if it does anything
  )
```

```{r}
plot
cap_print
cap_interactive
```
